title: Diagnostics & Troubleshooting
intro:
A node that is silently broken is worse than a node that is visibly offline. Your most important skill as a DevNet tester is the ability to read your node's logs, identify what is wrong, and either fix it yourself or document it precisely enough for the engineering team to reproduce it.

This module gives you a systematic approach to diagnosing the most common node failure modes.

sections.title: Reading Node Logs
sections.content:
LOG LEVELS
The PYRAX node emits structured logs at five severity levels. Learn to filter for what matters:

DEBUG: Very verbose. Shows every internal event. Only useful when you are tracing a specific, reproducible issue. Do not leave DEBUG logging on permanently — it generates gigabytes of data quickly.
INFO: Normal operational messages. Block imports, peer connections, consensus votes. A healthy node produces a steady stream of INFO messages every ~60 seconds.
WARN: Something unexpected happened but the node recovered automatically. Peer dropped, reconnected. Block arrived late. These are worth noting but not always reportable.
ERROR: A component failed. The node may have recovered, or may be in a degraded state. Always investigate ERROR entries.
FATAL / PANIC: The node has crashed or is about to crash. These always require an incident report.

KEY LOG KEYWORDS TO WATCH
IMPORTED BLOCK: The node successfully imported a new block. You should see this roughly every 60 seconds.
CONSENSUS VOTE: Your node cast a PoS vote. Only appears if you are staking.
FORK DETECTED: A competing chain tip was found. Normal occasionally, abnormal if it does not resolve.
PEER DISCONNECTED: A peer dropped. Normal occasionally. Abnormal if it happens continuously.
SLASHING DETECTED: Your validator double-signed. Immediate action required.
SYNC STALLED: The node has not imported a new block in an unexpected amount of time.
OUT OF DISK: Critical. The node will stop syncing if it runs out of disk space.

FILTERING LOGS IN PRACTICE
To watch only errors in real time:
journalctl -u pyraxd -f | grep -E 'ERROR|FATAL|PANIC'

To search the last 1000 lines for a specific keyword:
journalctl -u pyraxd -n 1000 | grep 'FORK_DETECTED'

sections.title: Common Issues & Fixes
sections.content:
NODE NOT SYNCING
Symptoms: No IMPORTED BLOCK messages for more than 5 minutes. Block height is stuck.
Diagnostic steps:
1. Check peer count: pyrax attach --exec 'net.peerCount'. If it is 0, you have a connectivity problem.
2. Check firewall: ensure port 30303 (TCP and UDP) is open both inbound and outbound.
3. Check disk space: df -h. If disk is full, the node cannot write new blocks.
4. Restart the daemon: systemctl restart pyraxd. Check if syncing resumes within 2 minutes.

NODE CRASHING (FATAL / PANIC)
Symptoms: FATAL or PANIC in logs. Process exits unexpectedly.
Diagnostic steps:
1. Capture the full stack trace from the log (the lines immediately following PANIC).
2. Note the exact node version: pyraxd --version.
3. Note the block height at the time of crash.
4. File a High or Critical incident report with all of the above.

OUT OF SYNC WITH NETWORK
Symptoms: Your node's block height is significantly behind peers. Peers show a higher chain head.
Diagnostic steps:
1. Check your internet connection speed and latency.
2. Increase peer connections if below minimum: edit pyrax.conf and increase maxpeers.
3. If more than 100 blocks behind: consider a full resync (pyraxd --resync). This is time-consuming but resolves database corruption.

HIGH MEMORY OR CPU USAGE
Symptoms: System is sluggish. Node process consuming excessive resources.
Diagnostic steps:
1. Check if you are running DEBUG logging — switch to INFO immediately.
2. Check if mempool is unusually large (flood of pending transactions during a stress test is expected).
3. If memory leak is suspected, restart the daemon and monitor over 24 hours. If it grows continuously, file a Medium incident report.

PORT CONFLICTS
Symptoms: Node fails to start. Logs show 'address already in use'.
Diagnostic steps:
1. Find what is using port 30303: netstat -tulpn | grep 30303 (Linux) or netstat -ano | findstr 30303 (Windows).
2. Stop the conflicting process or change the node's port in pyrax.conf.

quiz.question: A tester's node has not imported a new block for 8 minutes. The first diagnostic step is to check which of the following?
options: Restart the node immediately without any further investigation
File a Critical incident report straight away
Check peer count using pyrax attach --exec 'net.peerCount' to determine if there is a connectivity problem
Increase the maxpeers setting in pyrax.conf as the first action
quiz.explanation: The first step when a node stops syncing is to check peer count. Zero peers means a connectivity or firewall issue. Only if the peer count is healthy (and the node still isn't syncing) should you proceed to check disk space, restart the daemon, or file a report. Restarting blindly before diagnosing is a common mistake.

quiz.question: Which log level should you filter for to monitor only serious failures in real time?
options: DEBUG — because it captures the most detail and helps find the root cause faster
INFO — because it shows all normal block imports and peer connections
ERROR, FATAL, and PANIC — because these indicate component failures and crashes
WARN — because warnings always precede fatal failures and give early notice
quiz.explanation: ERROR, FATAL, and PANIC log levels indicate actual failures. DEBUG provides excessive volume and should only be used for specific tracing. INFO is for normal health monitoring. WARN messages are worth noting but represent automatic recoveries — they do not always precede fatal failures.

quiz.question: A node's log shows a PANIC entry followed by a stack trace, and the process has exited. What must the incident report include?
options: Only the date and time of the crash — the engineering team can find the rest
The full stack trace, exact node version, and block height at the time of the crash
A screenshot of the terminal and the tester's hardware specifications
A description of what the tester was doing on a different computer at the time
quiz.explanation: A PANIC is a high-severity crash. To reproduce and fix it, engineering needs: the full stack trace (exact error path), the node version (so they can locate the code), and the block height (to identify if a specific block triggered the crash). Without these, the report cannot be actioned.

quiz.question: A tester wants to check what process is using port 30303 on a Linux machine. Which command is correct?
options: ping 30303
ps aux | grep pyraxd
netstat -tulpn | grep 30303
systemctl status 30303
quiz.explanation: netstat -tulpn | grep 30303 lists all listening ports and filters for 30303, showing which process is bound to it. ping is for host reachability. ps aux lists processes by name, not port. systemctl status requires a service name, not a port number.

quiz.question: DEBUG logging is left enabled on a tester's node for a week. What is the most likely problem this causes?
options: The node runs faster because it processes fewer consensus messages
The node generates gigabytes of log data, which can fill the disk and cause the node to stop syncing
DEBUG logging has no side effects — it is safe to leave enabled indefinitely
It causes the node to reconnect to peers more frequently
quiz.explanation: DEBUG logging is extremely verbose and generates massive log files very quickly. If the disk fills up, the node cannot write new block data and will stop syncing (showing an OUT OF DISK log entry). Always use INFO level for production-like operation, and only switch to DEBUG temporarily when tracing a specific issue.
